Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
There is something wrong with me as a person
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette: Minh sat in a corner booth of a downtown bistro, his eyes fixed on the street. Years ago, in a windowless basement, interrogators had subjected him to systematic torture designed to unravel his sense of self. They would blast recordings of children screaming through rusted speakers, a sound that now made him jump violently at the clatter of silverware or the sudden ring of his own phone. Because these auditory triggers were so visceral, they instantly spiked his physical alarm, causing him to watch others closely for signs that they might harm him while flooding him with fear and shame. The overwhelming sensory reminders also fractured his recall, making it impossible for him to deliberately remember the sequence of events; when he tried, the narrative felt unreal, as though it belonged to a stranger. He had come to believe that his fractured recall was a sign that something was fundamentally defective about him as a person. This negative self-belief further distorted his memory, leaving large gaps where specific beatings or interrogations used to be, which in turn made him feel even more vulnerable to future harm. Because he felt exposed to others and convinced that his brokenness was visible to everyone, he began avoiding social contacts, steering clear of the friends he used to socialise with before the event. To cope, he also started to avoid eating or restrict food, a quiet coping habit that left him perpetually fatigued and emotionally numb. Over weeks, this undereating and isolation became his routine, but it only deepened his negative beliefs, convincing him he had acted against his own core values during the ordeal. The shame of his perceived failures made ordinary cues, like hearing a related name on a byline, instantly trigger another wave of panic. When he felt dizzy from skipping meals, the threat of collapsing in public felt inescapable, driving him to eat less and hide more. His active avoidance of social contacts and food meant he had no external anchors to help him reconstruct the timeline, which widened the memory gaps and made the traumatic story feel even more detached from reality. This fragmented recall left him without a coherent narrative, pushing him deeper into undereating and social withdrawal to conserve his dwindling energy. By isolating himself, he deprived himself of corrective exposure, which only made the remaining triggers feel more intense and unavoidable. The relentless state of threat made daily functioning impossible, so he retreated further into his coping habits, which drained his physical resilience and turned every minor stressor into a perceived danger. As a journalist, his career required him to sit in crowded newsrooms and interview sources, but the constant hum of office life now felt unbearable. Hearing a source's name during an interview would instantly spike his heart rate, making it impossible for him to focus on the story. He began missing deadlines, his reports growing short and disjointed, until his editor finally warned him about his declining performance. The occupational toll compounded his isolation, leaving him increasingly detached from his profession. Today, Minh sits in this booth not as a victim of the past, but as a man finally ready to break the cycle. He came to therapy because the isolation and occupational decline became unsustainable, and he fears that without intervention, he will lose his remaining connections entirely. He hopes to regain the ability to eat, to listen, and to trust that the world no longer holds the same terrifying weight.
